summary: A 1975 note with observations on the IMP and host protocol changes, drawing on international standards recommendations from IFIP working group 6.1. See also RFC 692, RFC 690 and RFC 687.

plainLanguage.summary: This note reviews a proposed packet label for connecting hosts to networks. It explains the label's fields and the difficulty of adding it to ARPANET's existing header.

subtitle: Comments on a proposed international packet header and its fit with ARPANET protocols.

tldr.problem: An international working group was considering a packet header for connecting hosts to packet networks, while ARPANET was changing its host interface.
tldr.mechanism: The note describes a proposed header made of network, format, type, facilities, text-length, and source and destination address fields, then considers how it could coexist with the existing Host-to-Host header.
tldr.outcome: The proposed 144-bit header plus a 40-bit Host-to-Host header totals 184 bits. The author lists possible ways to fit them, each with trade-offs.

sections.title: The International Proposal
sections.content:
Vinton Cerf's note responds to RFCs about IMP/Host and Host/IMP changes. It discusses a recommendation from working group 6.1 of the International Federation for Information Processing, which voted to present CCITT with a standard packet, or datagram, header.

The proposed header is for interfacing hosts to packet networks. It is neither a Host-to-Host header nor an IMP-to-IMP header. Its addressing fields use 96 bits, intended to match the telephone system's stated maximum address space.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed label connects a host to a packet network. It is a different layer from the labels used between hosts or between IMPs.

sections.title: Fields in the Proposed Header
sections.content:
The proposed fields are Local Network (4 bits), Datagram Format (4), Packet Type Code (8), Facilities (16), Text Length (16), Destination Address (48), and Source Address (48). The facilities bits had not been assigned, though the note mentions possible uses such as tracing, accounting, and class of service.

Text Length counts text octets but excludes the fixed-length header. Each address could contain network and host identifiers, an IMP identifier, and reserved bits. The note presents these as possible allocations, not as a finalized design.
sections.plainLanguage: The label has fields for network format, packet type, length, and both addresses. Some bits were still unassigned when the note was written.

sections.title: Fitting the Existing Header
sections.content:
The proposed packet header is 144 bits. Adding the then-current 40-bit Host-to-Host header produces 184 bits, which the author calls not very pleasant. One temporary idea removes the reserved 16-bit parts of both addresses to carry byte-size and byte-count information.

Other suggestions use the length field and a facilities bit, or add a dummy byte before the NCP header to make a 192-bit total. The note warns that the first alternatives require substantial changes to NCP programs. It also questions whether a bit-length field is needed when most data uses 8-bit quantities, while acknowledging machines with 36-bit and 32-bit words.
sections.plainLanguage: Combining the new label with the old one makes an awkward total size. The author offers several possible adjustments, but none is cost-free.
